hero.name: Divya
hero.who: a home baker in Jaipur whose long to-do list never gets shorter

story.b: Divya bakes cakes and cookies from her flat in Malviya Nagar, Jaipur, and her to-do list lives on the fridge door. Today it has forty-two items. Post three reels. Try a gulab jamun cheesecake. Redesign the boxes. Reply to forty messages. Fix the accounts. Build a website. Order butter paper. Somewhere in the middle, in tiny letters, is reply to Cafe Neelam, a busy cafe near the university that asked about weekly orders three weeks ago. Divya works from seven in the morning until eleven at night. She ticks off small things all day, and the list never shrinks. Her husband Vikram finds her asleep on the sofa with a piping bag in her hand. The cafe email is still unanswered.

ask.q: Divya works sixteen hours a day but nothing big moves. What should she change first?
o: Work faster so she can finish more of the forty-two items
Find the one task that would make most of the others easier
Add a second list so she can track everything properly
ask.why: Working faster on a flat list still treats every item as equal, and a second list just adds more to manage. Asking which single task would make the rest easier or unnecessary points her straight at the email that could change her business.

chapters.take: A long list feels busy. One right task actually moves you.

story.b: On Monday, over a cup of masala chai, Divya stops looking at the fridge. She asks herself one question instead: which single thing, if she did it today, would make the most other things easier? The answer is embarrassingly clear. A steady weekly order from Cafe Neelam would pay for the butter, the boxes and the instalments on her new oven. It would also mean fewer random orders to chase online. She writes the cafe owner a short reply and bakes a sample box of her three best brownies. By Thursday the owner calls. He wants sixty brownies every week. Divya looks at the fridge again. Half the items on it suddenly do not matter much.

ask.q: Next Monday Divya's list is long again. What is her best first move?
o: Start with the quickest items to build some momentum
Answer whichever customer message arrives first
Ask which single task would make the rest easier, and do that first
ask.why: Quick items feel satisfying but rarely change much, and answering messages in order lets other people set her priorities. The focusing question cuts through the list and finds the one task that makes many others easier or unnecessary.

chapters.take: Ask what one thing would make everything else easier. Start there.

story.b: In the first week of the cafe order, Divya tries to do everything at once. The brownie batter is mixing, a customer is asking about a birthday cake on WhatsApp, her mother is on speakerphone about a cousin's wedding, and a cooking show plays on the laptop. She forgets the timer. The whole first tray comes out black at the edges. She has to start again at ten at night. The next day she tries something different. Phone face down in the bedroom. Laptop shut. For ninety minutes she only bakes. Then she spends twenty minutes on messages, fully. The brownies come out perfect, and to her surprise the messages take less time when she gives them her whole attention too.

ask.q: Divya's friend Meera, a teacher, grades papers while chatting on the family group and watching TV. What would help her finish faster?
o: Grade with every other screen off, then reply to the group afterwards
Keep everything on, since switching keeps her from getting bored
Grade papers only late at night when the group is quiet
ask.why: Doing several things at once really means switching back and forth, and every switch costs focus and time. Keeping everything on feels lively but slows her down. Waiting for late night just moves the problem. One task with full attention gets it done.

chapters.take: Doing three things at once usually means doing three things badly.

story.b: Divya sits down with a pencil and does something she has never done. She takes the whole fridge list and ranks it by how much each item would actually help the business. Most of it lands at the bottom. Redesigning the boxes, a fancy website, a new cheesecake flavour. Near the top are three things: keep the cafe happy, find a second cafe, and call the offices near Tonk Road about Diwali hampers. She had been spending two hours a day on reels that brought maybe one order a week. Now she spends that time on five phone calls. One software office orders two hundred hampers. Divya circles the top item every morning and lets the rest wait.

ask.q: A friend who runs a small tiffin service spends hours arranging his Instagram page. What should he do?
o: Keep posting daily, since being seen is everything
Rank his tasks by impact and spend his best hours on the few that bring most orders
Give every task equal time so nothing is neglected
ask.why: Treating every task as equal spreads his time thin, and posting daily may feel productive while bringing little. Ranking tasks by real impact shows the handful that drive most of his results, so the small stuff can wait without harm.

chapters.take: A few tasks drive most results. Find them and let the rest wait.

story.b: Divya's best energy comes early, but her mornings keep getting eaten. A neighbour drops in for chai. Her mother-in-law needs help finding a document. A supplier calls about a delivery. By noon she is tired and has done nothing important. So she blocks seven to ten every morning for the cafe batch and sales calls, and treats it like a meeting she cannot miss. She tells Vikram and his mother, and sticks a note on the kitchen door. On the third day, an aunt arrives unannounced at eight thirty. Vikram happily makes the tea and keeps her company. Divya joins them at ten, with sixty brownies cooling and two new cafe meetings booked. The aunt praises the brownies.

ask.q: During Divya's protected morning, a neighbour wants a quick chat at eight. What should she do?
o: Chat now, since it is rude to refuse a neighbour
Give up the block on days when people visit
Kindly say she is busy until ten and offer to meet after
ask.why: Saying yes every time quietly turns the block back into ordinary free time, and dropping it on busy days means it disappears whenever life gets noisy. A kind no with a later time protects the work and still respects the neighbour.

chapters.take: Guard one block of time for your most important work, every day.

story.b: October turns into a blur of cocoa and cardboard. With the cafe orders and three hundred Diwali hampers, Divya knows she cannot keep a neat balance this month. She talks it through with Vikram. For four weeks, the business comes first. He handles school pickups for their daughter Tara, and Divya skips her kitty party and her evening walks. But she keeps two things safe: seven hours of sleep and dinner with the family. The day after Diwali, she shuts the oven for a full week. They take the train to Udaipur, eat at a small lakeside dhaba and do nothing at all. Divya catches up on sleep. Tara gets her mother back, and the business is still there when they return.

ask.q: After the busy season, Divya is tempted to take on a big new order straight away. What would be wisest?
o: Rest and give family time first, then plan the next push
Take the order now, since momentum must never stop
Never go out of balance again, and keep every month equally busy
ask.why: Big results often need a period of heavy focus, but staying out of balance too long wears down health and family. Keeping every month equal blocks the big pushes. Deliberately swinging back to rest and family after the rush lets her lean in again later.

chapters.take: Lean hard into what matters for a season, then come back to rest.

story.b: By the new year, the list on Divya's fridge has five items, not forty-two. She bakes for three cafes now, and the office orders came back for Christmas. Every morning she still asks her one question over chai, and from seven to ten the kitchen door stays closed. Her phone lives in the bedroom while she bakes. The box redesign she once worried about never happened, and nobody seems to mind. Some weeks are busy and lopsided, and she lets them be, because she knows a quiet week is coming. Vikram notices that she laughs more at dinner. Tara has started making her own to-do lists for school, and asks her mother which item matters most.

chapters.take: Fewer priorities, guarded well, built more than a busy list ever did.
